title: The 12 key UX metrics to evaluate and improve the user experience
description: SUPR-Q, SUS, NPS, SEQ and more: the 12 key tools to measure the user experience, with the purpose and an example of each.
updateNote: Revised in October 2026: I added what has changed since publication and a new visual to explain the core idea.

related.title: Clint Acquire
related.body: In practice: a landing page and a conversational flow that captured 79% of the sales demand.

blocks.text: Evaluating the user experience isn't a luxury. It's a necessity if you want to build digital products that truly connect with people. If you want to better understand how your users perceive your product, these 12 tools are essential. Let's break each one down and show how it can be applied in day-to-day design work.
SUPR-Q: Measuring Trust and Usability
Evaluate usability, trust, loyalty and overall appearance.
An e-commerce store compares its site with competitors using SUPR-Q to find out whether the design feels trustworthy and easy to navigate.
It has 8 items that roll up into four factors: usability, trust, appearance and loyalty. Because it's standardized, you can compare your site with others that used the same questionnaire.

blocks.caption: The 8 items become four factors. The lowest factor shows where the experience loses strength.

blocks.text: SUS: Quick Usability Assessment
A 10-item scale to measure usability quickly.
A digital bank uses SUS after launching a new feature to find out whether customers can use it easily.

There are 10 statements answered from 1 to 5, alternating positive and negative phrasing. For the positive ones, subtract 1 from the answer; for the negative ones, subtract the answer from 5. The sum multiplied by 2.5 becomes a score from 0 to 100. The most widely used benchmark average is 68.

blocks.caption: From questionnaire to score: each answer becomes points, and the sum times 2.5 is compared with the benchmark average of 68.

blocks.text: NPS: Measuring Customer Loyalty
Measures how likely customers are to recommend your product.
After a purchase, an e-commerce store sends an NPS survey to gauge customer satisfaction and loyalty.

A single question, from 0 to 10. A 9 or 10 is a promoter, a 7 or 8 is passive, and 0 to 6 is a detractor. NPS is the percentage of promoters minus the percentage of detractors, and it ranges from −100 to 100.

blocks.caption: Each answer falls into one of three groups. Passives don't count in the math.

blocks.text: SEQ: Measuring Task Difficulty
A single question to measure how difficult a specific task is.
An accounting firm uses SEQ to find out whether clients can generate financial reports without trouble.
Right after each task, the person answers one question from 1 (very difficult) to 7 (very easy). Comparing scores across tasks shows where the flow gets stuck.

blocks.caption: One question per task. The task with the lowest score is the first to investigate.

blocks.text: UMUX/UMUX-LITE: An Alternative to SUS
A compact assessment of perceived usability.
A media company runs UMUX-LITE to test how readers receive a new layout on its news portal.

UMUX-LITE uses just two statements, from 1 to 7: whether the features meet the person's needs and whether it's easy to use. It's short enough to fit at the end of any session and usually tracks SUS results well.

blocks.caption: Two questions and one score. Ideal when you can't ask respondents for more time.

blocks.text: WAMMI: Satisfaction in Complex Environments
Evaluates user satisfaction on complex or high-traffic websites.
A social network uses WAMMI to measure how users react to interface changes.

There are 20 statements about the site, summarized into five dimensions: attractiveness, control, efficiency, helpfulness and learnability. The result shows the profile of the experience, not just a score.

blocks.caption: The statements form a profile across five dimensions. The sunken dimension is the weak spot.

blocks.text: PSSUQ: System Quality and Usefulness
Measures the user experience in specific usage scenarios.
A SaaS platform uses PSSUQ to find out whether its integration settings are easy for users.
The current version has 16 items, from 1 to 7, split into three subscales: system usefulness, information quality and interface quality. Here the logic is reversed: the lower the score, the better.

blocks.caption: Three subscales, where lower is better. Splitting the score shows whether the problem is the interface or the information.

blocks.text: SUMI: In-Depth Software Evaluation
A detailed 50-item software evaluation.
An IT company runs SUMI to test the usability of its ERP among corporate clients.

There are 50 items answered with agree, undecided or disagree, grouped into five subscales: efficiency, affect, helpfulness, control and learnability. It's long, but it gives a detailed picture of complex software.

blocks.caption: Many items, five subscales. Worth the effort when the software is used all day long.

blocks.text: QUIS: Satisfaction with Digital Interfaces
Evaluates feedback, learning and engagement with interfaces.
A learning app uses QUIS to measure what students think about navigating its interactive lessons.
It uses pairs of opposite words on 1 to 9 scales, organized by parts of the interface, such as screen, terminology, learning and system capabilities.

blocks.caption: Each part of the interface gets its own scale, and it becomes clear which one gets in the way the most.

blocks.text: PURE: Prioritizing Usability in Essential Tasks
Focuses on how easy the main tasks are.
A logistics company uses PURE to check how drivers access critical information, such as delivery status and routes.
It's not a user questionnaire. Experts break the task into steps and rate each one 1 (easy), 2 (some effort) or 3 (difficult). The sum is the task score, and the lower, the better.

blocks.caption: Each step gets a 1, 2 or 3. The red step is the first one to redesign.

blocks.text: NASA-TLX: Measuring Workload
Evaluates cognitive and physical load.
A hospital uses NASA-TLX to measure the impact of its electronic health record system on nurses' workload.

It measures workload across six dimensions, from 0 to 100: mental demand, physical demand, time pressure, performance, effort and frustration. It's widely used to compare a current system with a new version.

blocks.caption: The six dimensions, before and after. The drop shows how much weight the new system took off the people using it.

blocks.text: UEQ: Quick Usability and UX Assessment
Quickly captures aspects of the user experience.
A streaming app uses UEQ to measure how intuitive search and filters feel in its movie catalog.

There are 26 pairs of opposite adjectives, from 1 to 7, grouped into six scales: attractiveness, perspicuity, efficiency, dependability, stimulation and novelty. It covers both the practical and the emotional side of the experience.

blocks.caption: One adjective pair from each scale. You can see that a product can be pleasing and still feel slow.

blocks.text: How to choose the right metric
Twelve metrics is a lot. The most common mistake is picking the most famous one instead of the one that answers the team's question.
Two questions help you decide: am I evaluating a specific task or the whole product? And how much time can the person spend answering?

blocks.caption: Start with the question. Each question lights up the questionnaire that answers it, from a single task to the whole product.

blocks.text: Questionnaires measure perception. To understand behavior, combine them with usage data, such as completion rate, time on task and drop-off by step.
Today AI helps a lot with grouping open-ended answers and finding themes. But the score and the interpretation need to be reviewed by someone on the team, especially with small samples.
Why do these tools matter?

They're like thermometers for the user experience. Applied correctly, they help you tune your product to: Ensure usability. Strengthen user loyalty. Prioritize improvements that truly impact the experience.

blocks.caption: Metrics are thermometers for the experience.

blocks.text: What about you? Have you used any of these metrics? Which one gave you the most valuable insights? Let's swap ideas in the comments!
